[MUQATIL:71:15-20/r4] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | People's first creation was from earth's soil; nabatan means creation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءالمصدرفيهعلىغيرالفعللأنالمعنىواحد)#692/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A verbal noun can follow a different verb pattern when the meanings match: أنبتكم نباتا is justified because أنبته is equivalent to قد نبت.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءالمصدرفيهعلىغيرالفعللأنالمعنىواحد)#692/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same equivalence licenses اجتوروا تجاورا and تجاوروا اجتوارا, as well as انكسر كسرا and كسر انكسارا.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءالمصدرفيهعلىغيرالفعللأنالمعنىواحد)#692/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · ابن مسعود | reports | A reading attributed to Ibn Masعود has وأنزل الملائكة تنزيلا, since أنزل and نزل share a meaning. | mentions 25:25
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماجاءالمصدرفيهعلىغيرالفعللأنالمعنىواحد)#692/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Al-Qatami’s تتبعه اتباعا and Ruʾba’s تطويت انطواء show paired verbs with equivalent meanings; يدعه تركا is similar because يدع and يترك mean the same.
[AKHFASH:v2p550/r4] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | He treats نبات as a verbal noun for the action, while identifying الإنبات as the regular verbal noun; نبات conveys the same meaning.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p229/r8] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | Nabātan is a cognate accusative by meaning: anbata means “made you grow”; inbātan is the regular verbal noun, while nabātan is more emphatic.
[NAHHAS:v5p39/r3] NAHHAS, d. 338 · author | holds | The verbal noun of أنبت is إنبات; the construction is paraphrased as “He caused you to grow as a plant.”
[NAHHAS:v5p39/r4] NAHHAS, d. 338 · قيل | reports | One explanation connects the verse to Adam's creation from clay.
[NAHHAS:v5p39/r5] NAHHAS, d. 338 · قيل | reports | Another explanation says the sperm drop is created from earth.
[THALABI:v10p44#2/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | Nabātan is used where the expected verbal noun would be inbātan; it is a verbal noun differing from its regular form.
[THALABI:v10p44#2/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl paraphrases the phrase as ‘you grew from the earth, growing.’
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p101/r22] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says this refers to Adam, created from the soil of the whole earth.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p101/r23] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · خالد بن معدان | reports | Khalid ibn Maʿdan says the human was created from clay and remarks that hearts soften in winter.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p101/r24] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن بحر | reports | Ibn Baḥr takes the growth to describe development from smallness to largeness and from shortness to height.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v6p101/r25] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Al-Mawardi also allows that all creatures originate by nourishment from the earth's growth and substances.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p260/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās takes this as the beginning of Adam’s creation from the earth.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p260/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الكلبي | reports | Adam was created from the earth, and people are his descendants.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p260/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · مقاتل | reports | The phrase means the beginning of your creation from the earth’s dust.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p260/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأخفش | reports | Al-Akhfash says the noun nabātan stands in place of the verbal noun inbāt, conveying the same sense.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p260/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أبو إسحاق | reports | Abū Isḥāq treats nabātan as a semantic verbal noun: anbatakum means He made you grow; the wording about your growing is more emphatic.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:71:15-18/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | God made humanity sprout from earth: He created Adam from earth and his living descendants from him.
[DAMGHANI:v1p447/r6] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | Anbata can mean to create; God created humankind from the earth.
[JISHUMI:v10p7097/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | إنبات is bringing a plant out of the earth through gradual growth, stage by stage.
[JISHUMI:v10p7097/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil parses نباتا as a verbal noun with a form unlike its verb's usual مصدر إنباتا, estimating أنبتكم فنبتم نباتا.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p231#2/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | The verse points to Adam's origin: God created him from earth, and people are his descendants.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p231#2/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | Nabātan is used in place of verbal noun inbātan.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p231#2/r4] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl paraphrases this as God making you grow, so that you grew as growth.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p374#2/r17] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Growing humanity from earth is a metaphor: Adam was taken from earth, and all people grew from him.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p374#2/r18] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Nabātan is a verbal noun formed from a different source than the finite verb; the implied wording is fa-nabattum nabātan.
[TABRISI:71:15-17/r13] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Nabatan is an accusative verbal noun from an omitted verb, anbatakum fanabattum; al-Zajjaj says it follows the sense, since anbatakum means made you grow.
[TABRISI:71:15-17/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abu Amr reads mimma khatayahum with yāʾ; the other readers have khatiʾatihim with tāʾ, lengthening, and hamza.
[TABRISI:71:15-17/r20] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Humanity's original creation began with Adam, who was made from earth, and all people descend from him. | mentions 4:1
[TABRISI:71:15-17/r3] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The commentary says it discussed the variant in waladuhu in Surat Maryam. | mentions 19:77
[TABRISI:71:18-23/r1] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | Another explanation is that God originated everyone through nourishment from what the earth grows and what grows within it.
[TABRISI:71:18-23/r2] TABRISI, d. 548 · قيل | reports | A further explanation describes growth from smallness to old age and from shortness to height.
[TABRISI:71:18-23/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | These favors show that God alone deserves worship without association, knows people's interests, and wisely governs them; people should not answer His blessings with disbelief and denial.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p581/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | reports | Nabāt can mean creation or origination from the earth.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p581/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The verbal noun nabāt is parsed as the object of an omitted verb: God made you grow, so you grew; likewise, He nurtured her and she grew. | mentions 3:37
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Humanity’s initial creation from the earth refers to Adam.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalil paraphrases the phrase as you grew as plants.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الزجاج | reports | Al-Zajjaj says nabātan is a verbal noun used according to the sense, since anbatakum means made you grow.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba notes a verbal noun formed differently from its verb, comparing tabtīlan from tabattala and referring to 73:8. | mentions 73:8
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r5] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الشاعر | reports | An unnamed poet uses ittibāʿan as a verbal noun associated with the verb ittabiʿta, illustrating nonmatching verbal-noun forms.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r6] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · الشاعر الآخر | reports | A second unnamed poet’s ʿiwādan illustrates the same kind of verbal-noun formation.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p371#4/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن قتيبة | reports | Ibn Qutayba generalizes that verbal nouns can differ in form from their verbs because differently formed verbs may share one meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse returns to proofs within human selves and explains the creation in stages: humans are made from earth, returned to it, then brought out again. | mentions 71:14
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One interpretation takes the address as referring to Adam, the ancestor whom God grew from the earth, as with Adam's creation from dust. | mentions 3:59
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second interpretation says God grew all people from earth indirectly: nutrients produce plants, plants produce food, and food produces semen.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The wording is elliptical: God caused you to grow, and you then grew as a remarkable growth, rather than the expected verbal noun meaning an act of growing.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling the growth wondrous makes the proof perceptible: God's act itself is unseen and would require revelation to establish, while the complete, marvelous plant growth can be observed.
[RAZI-FULL:v30p124/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The growth of people from the earth, their return to it, and their emergence again form the third proof of God's oneness.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r1] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj says Adam was created from the soil of the whole earth; Qurtubi refers to his earlier discussion in al-Anʿam and al-Baqara.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r2] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · خالد بن معدان | reports | Khalid ibn Maʿdan says humans were created from clay and that hearts therefore soften in winter.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r3] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Nabatan is a noun placed where the verbal noun would be: the verbal noun of anbata is inbat.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r4] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · الخليل، الزجاج | reports | Al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj treat nabatan as a verbal noun based on the meaning: God made people grow with a growing.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r5] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | reports | Another reading of the syntax is 'He grew plants for you from the eart

h,' making nabatan an explicit cognate accusative; Qurtubi says the first analysis is clearer.
[QURTUBI-FULL:71:17-18/r6] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · ابن جريج | reports | Ibn Jurayj also explains that God caused human beings to grow on earth, increasing them from childhood to adulthood and from shortness to height.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:71:15-19/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Growing is a metaphor for originating humans from earth because it better conveys their coming into being and formation from it; the fuller construction is abridged by entailment.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:71:15-19/r4] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | The implied fuller wording is 'He caused you to grow from earth, then you grew'; the verse compresses this by relying on entailment.
[NASAFI-FULL:v4p284/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | God brought people into existence from earth, using the metaphor of a plant's growth; thus they grew like plants.
[QASHANI:71:15-20/r4] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | God’s growing people from the earth means their emergence from the earth of the body.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p283/r10] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | rejects | The author says he cannot understand al-Zamakhshari’s second grammatical explanation.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p283/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Inbāt is metaphorical for creation: Adam was created from earth and his descendants came from him, so all humans may be said to have been grown from it.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p283/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Nabātan is accusative as a verbal noun with the extra letters deleted, meaning inbātan.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p283/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another parsing supplies an omitted verb: fa-nabattum, “then you grew.”
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p283/r9] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Al-Zamakhshari also says the phrase means “He grew you, and you grew,” or makes nabātan accusative because anbatakum contains the sense of nabattum.
[SAMIN-DURR:71:17/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | نباتا can be a verbal noun from أنبت with its extra letters removed, a so-called اسم مصدر.
[SAMIN-DURR:71:17/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Alternatively it is accusative under an implicit نبتم; al-Zamakhshari says أنبتكم contains this sense, and al-Samin identifies this with the omitted-growth analysis.
[SAMIN-DURR:71:17/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The verb of growing people from earth is a strong metaphor.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p234/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Nabātan here is a verbal noun, a particularly apt form for describing God making humanity grow from the earth.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p234/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Noah invokes God's creative power and greatness and His heavenly and earthly benefits: God provides, made the sky a structure and earth a resting place, and expanded provision.
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p234/r5] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Because God alone creates and provides without peer, equal, partner, spouse, child, minister, or adviser, He alone must be worshipped.
[BURHAN:v2p393/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | In ‘I planted them with a planting,’ نباتا is not the true verbal noun of أنبت; the proper مصدر is الإنبات, while نبات names the result, like الكلام and السلام beside التكليم and التسليم.
[BURHAN:v2p393/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | The object of أسررت is omitted and understood as supplication, warning, and the like; source-like emphasis can coexist with this ellipsis because the source form is not always used for literal emphasis.
[BURHAN:v2p393/r5] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Two explanations reconcile إسرارا with the omitted object: it supplies a rhyme rather than emphasis, or أسررت is treated as intransitive after its object is disregarded, like ‘he gives and withholds.’
[BURHAN:v2p393/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Emphasis may use a synonym rather than the verb’s own source: جهارا is a kind of الدعاء, ليا a kind of distortion, and perhaps بهتانا a kind of wrongdoing.
[BURHAN:v2p397/r3] BURHAN, d. 794 · المبرد | reports | Al-Mubarrad analyzes nabāt as governed by an omitted verb, meaning God made you grow from the earth and you grew; Ibn Khuruf chose this, Ibn Yaʿish agreed, and it was attributed to Sibawayh.
[BURHAN:v2p397/r4] BURHAN, d. 794 · ابن عصفور | rejects | Ibn ʿAsfur disputes the claim that the omitted-verb analysis is Sibawayh's position.
[BURHAN:v2p397/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Zarkashi distinguishes meanings: when the noun differs from the verb, an implied verb governs it, since a noncognate noun cannot emphasize or clarify that verb; when meanings match, the overt verb may govern it.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p162#s071/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The sūra's aim is to show God's complete power to destroy those warned and replace them with better people, and to bring about the Resurrection that they deny; Noah's story establishes the threat through his people's destruction for rejecting him.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p162#s071/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The basmala describes God as wholly perfect in majesty and generosity, universally giving outward blessings as al-Raḥmān, and granting His obedient allies lasting blessing as al-Raḥīm.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p171/r10] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The wording uses iḥtibāk: anbatakum implies a deleted first verbal noun, while the explicit second noun implies a deleted second verb, yielding anbatakum inbātan fa-nabattum nabātan.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p171/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After the heavens, Biqāʿī returns to human creation, the greatest created thing and clearest sign of God, now specifying its details while explicitly establishing resurrection through a plant-growth metaphor.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p171/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | God grew humans from earth by creating their father Adam; the plant image recalls Adam's earthly origin and humanity's formation from earth.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p171/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The earth also supplies human food; people grow through that nourishment from the same earth from which they were created.
[BIQAI-FULL:v8p171/r9] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Nabātan is a verbal noun used where the verb would ordinarily appear; stripping the augmented form signals how easy this creative origination is for God despite its wondrous novelty.
[DURR-FULL:v8p291/r7] DURR-FULL, d. 911 · ابن جريج | reports | Adam was created from the soil of the whole earth.
[ITQAN:v3p178/r6] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Emphasis may use a verbal noun from another verb or a concrete noun instead of a verbal noun: “vegetation” means “growing.”
[BURSEVI:v10p137/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Humanity was wondrously brought from earth, either through the creation of their father Adam from it or through the chain of sperm, plants, and earthly food.
[BURSEVI:v10p137/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | Nabātan is an emphatic verbal noun or noun of action in place of inbātan, confirming anbatakum; the following ikh r ājan likewise supports this construction.
[BURSEVI:v10p137/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · بعضهم | reports | Another analysis takes nabātan as a circumstantial accusative, indicating that humans are plantlike in earthly origin and growth, though they have an additional quality.
[BURSEVI:v10p137/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · أهل المعرفة | reports | People of spiritual knowledge read the verse as saying that bodily nourishment and growth come from the earth, as plants grow through water and soil.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | God created you from the earth; plant growth is a metaphor for origination because it vividly shows coming into being from earth, an observable process.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الخفاجي | reports | Al-Khafaji objects that al-Qadi's account misses the rhetorical indication already described.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The metaphor is an explicit, transferred verbal metaphor; deniers of resurrection are treated as though they also denied origination.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Min is an originative preposition referring to the remote source of creation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · أبو حيان وجماعة | reports | Abu Hayyan and others parse nabātan as an emphatic verbal noun for anbattukum, with the extra letters removed from the underlying form.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | Another parse supplies an omitted verb: fa-nabattum nabātan, you therefore grew as a plant.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · صاحب الكشف | reports | The Kashf argues that inbāt and nabāt differ only in whether the act is viewed from agent or recipient, so no extra verb is needed; if inbāt keeps its lexical sense, it already entails growth.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | If anbata means the conventional preliminary planting of a seed, the implied growth signals God's power and swift decree, as in 7:160. | mentions 7:160
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A further analysis reconstructs an original pair, anbatakum inbātan fa-nabattum nabātan, then omits the verbal noun from the first clause and the verb from the second by ellipsis.
[ALUSI-FULL:v29p75#3/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · القاضي | reports | Al-Qadi says the wording is abbreviated because its meaning is supplied by entailment.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Nabat and nabt can be a collective noun for anything growing from the earth, conventionally especially grass or fodder, or a verbal noun meaning sprouting and growing; anbata means to make grow or bring forth.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Growth is the distinguishing feature of vegetation, manifested through nourishment and reproduction.

ELMALILI:71:17-20/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · المفسرون | reports | Commentators take nabatan as a cognate accusative rather than a circumstantial accusative because it is originally a verbal noun and human life is not simply plant life.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · بعض المفسرين | reports | One grammatical explanation treats nabatan directly as the cognate accusative of anbata, with the sense that God raised you by growing you from the earth.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · بعض المفسرين | reports | Another explanation makes nabatan the resultative verbal noun of an implied triliteral verb: God caused you to grow, and you grew a growth.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · الرازي | reports | Al-Razi gives two senses: God first created humanity through Adam from soil, as in 3:59, or created all people from the earth through seed, food, and plants that ultimately come from earth. | mentions 3:59
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı endorses the point that the unusual wording makes human growth directly observable, allowing it to serve as evidence of God’s perfect power rather than requiring reliance only on revelation.
[ELMALILI:71:17-20/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | Even if nabatan is taken as a circumstantial phrase the nuance remains, but commentators prefer its basic verbal-noun sense as a cognate accusative, which is prior and stronger than the circumstantial construction.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r1] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | After the argument from the heavens, Noah turns to the earth and its striking cycle of death and burial, preceded by the creation of people.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r2] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The passage teaches that humans are formed from earth's elements like plants and embeds the promise of life after death.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | أنبتكم means “created you,” likening human creation to plant growth; the resemblance is especially close because humans are made from earth's elements, as in 3:37 and the idiom “God planted you for good.” | mentions 3:37
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r4] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · قيل | reports | An unnamed view takes the implied meaning as “He grew your ancestor,” namely Adam, created from dust in 3:59. | mentions 3:59
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r5] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | نباتا is a verbal noun from أنبت treated as an emphatic direct object, rather than the regular إنباتا.
[IBNASHUR-FULL:v29p204/r6] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The lighter, established نباتا is preferred over the heavier إنباتا as a mark of eloquence.
